title: The Brahmin Who Walked on the River (TA)
summary: An ascetic boasts that thirty years of meditation gave him the power to walk across the river Yamuna. Birbal shows him the true market value of his 'miracle.'
full_text:
A proud hermit named Sadhu Jalandhar arrived at Emperor Akbar's court, surrounded by awestruck followers. The hermit proclaimed:

'I have performed severe penance in the high Himalayas for thirty long years! I have mastered the secret art of levitation! I can walk across the deep river Yamuna upon the surface of the water without sinking, as if walking upon stone! Does Your Majesty's court possess any power that can match my divine miracle?'

Akbar was fascinated and went with Birbal and the court to the banks of the Yamuna to witness the demonstration.

Before thousands of spectators, the hermit chanted mantras, stepped onto the flowing water, and walked across the wide river to the opposite bank without sinking, stepping ashore with completely dry feet!

The crowd gasped in mystical awe. Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Birbal! He walked across the river! Thirty years of meditation to achieve such a wonder! Is it not priceless?'

Birbal walked to the river pier, approached an ordinary boatman who was rowing a wooden ferry across the river, and asked:

'Brother boatman, how much do you charge to carry a traveler across the Yamuna in your boat?'

The boatman smiled humbly: 'Two copper dams, my lord. Just two small coppers.'

Birbal returned to Emperor Akbar and the proud hermit with a radiant smile:

'Sire, I have just calculated the exact value of this holy man's thirty years of meditation!

'It is worth exactly two copper dams!

'For two copper dams, this humble boatman carries merchants, women, children, and sacks of wheat across the river safely every day, feeding his family through honest labor!

'This ascetic spent thirty years of his precious human life in cold caves, doing nothing for society, healing no sick, feeding no hungry, merely to save himself two copper dams at the river ferry!

'What a tragic waste of human life to spend thirty years acquiring a parlor trick that a boatman outperforms for two pennies!'

The entire crowd roared with laughter. The hermit blushed with profound shame, realizing that vanity had hijacked his spiritual journey, and Akbar thanked Birbal for separating genuine virtue from empty spectacles.
moral: நீதி மற்றும் வாழ்க்கை பாடம்: Wit beats power
